Abstract
Motivated by applications in entanglement-assisted quantum error-correcting
codes (EA-QECCs), where the hull dimension of a code provides the required number
of pre-shared entangled pairs, we study the hull of two families of Fq-linear codes
defined by q-polynomial operators over Fqm using a unified Gram-matrix approach.
For image codes C(α) = im Φα(x), where Φα = P
i αiFi is a linear combination of
fixed q-polynomials, our master hull–rank theorem establishes dim Hull(C(α)) =
rank(Φα) −rank(G(α)), with G(α) being the associated Gram matrix over Fq.
Specializing to the two-parameter family Cλ,µ = im ϕλ,µ, where ϕλ,µ(x) = λx+µL(x),
yields a quadratic pencil λ2G0 + λµG1 + µ2G2 whose determinant governs the
LCD locus in P1(Fq).
In a parallel setting for Fqm-linear rank-distance codes
C = ⟨X, F1, . . . , Fk⟩Fqm equipped with the Delsarte inner product, an analogous
k × k Gram matrix over Fqm directly determines the hull dimension. Focusing on
the Frobenius twist L(X) = Xqk with d = gcd(k, m), the circulant structure of the
Gram matrices yields a closed-form discriminant and a complete classification in
three of the four bijectivity configurations over P1(Fqm). In the residual case, we
show the hull dimension equals δ = dimFq(im ϕλ,µ ∩ker ϕ†
λ,µ), and characterize the
extremal case δ = d via an explicit trace-isotropy criterion. Finally, we derive an
explicit count of LCD versus non-LCD points, proving that the LCD locus density
approaches 1 as q →∞. All theoretical results are supported by a worked example
over F64 and a SageMath verification provided in the appendix.

hull dimension is a fundamental invariant of a linear code: Hull(C) = {0} characterizes
linear complementary dual (LCD) codes, C ⊆C⊥characterizes self-orthogonal codes, and
C = C⊥characterizes self-dual codes.
LCD codes were introduced by Massey [16], who showed that they are asymptotically
good and provide an optimal solution to the two-user binary adder channel. Sendrier [17]
subsequently proved that LCD codes meet the asymptotic Gilbert–Varshamov bound.
Interest in the hull was renewed by the work of Carlet and Guilley [7], who demonstrated
that binary LCD codes offer effective resistance against side-channel and fault injection
attacks in hardware implementations of symmetric-key cryptography. This observation
initiated an intensive study of LCD codes and, more broadly, of codes with prescribed hull
dimension over finite fields [9, 8, 12].
The relationship between the hull and quantum error correction is equally direct.
Calderbank and Shor [6] and, independently, Steane [18] showed that self-orthogonal codes
give rise to quantum stabilizer codes via the CSS construction. The subsequent theory of
entanglement-assisted quantum error-correcting codes (EA-QECCs), developed by Brun,
Devetak, and Hsieh [5], extends this to arbitrary linear codes at the cost of pre-shared
entanglement. Guenda, Jitman, and Gulliver [12] made the connection precise: the number
of entangled pairs required to construct an EA-QECC from a classical code equals the hull
dimension of that code. Controlling the hull thus amounts to controlling the entanglement
cost.
In the rank-metric setting, rank-distance codes were introduced by Delsarte [10] and,
independently, by Gabidulin [11], who constructed the family of maximum rank distance
(MRD) codes now bearing his name. These codes can be defined using q-polynomials
(linearized polynomials), and their duality theory uses the Delsarte inner product on
coefficient vectors. The hull of a rank-metric code with respect to the Delsarte dual has
received increasing attention in recent years [13], prompted by the same quantum coding
applications that drove the Hamming-metric hull theory.

Conclusions and open problems
In this paper we developed a unified Gram-matrix approach for computing the hull of
two families of linearized polynomial codes over Fqm. The master hull–rank theorem
(Theorem 3.1) reduces the problem to a rank comparison between an operator and its
associated Gram matrix, yielding explicit LCD and self-orthogonality criteria in both
the image-code and rank-distance settings. For the Frobenius twist L(X) = Xqk, the
circulant structure of the Gram matrices leads to an explicit closed-form analysis: the
non-LCD locus within P1(Fq) is controlled by a degree-2m discriminant, three of the four
bijectivity configurations admit exact hull formulas, and the residual case (ε1, ε2) = (1, 1)
18


is reduced to the intersection im ϕλ,µ ∩ker ϕ†
λ,µ, with the extremal value d characterized
by Proposition 6.11.
Several natural directions remain open. It would be valuable to extend the Gram-matrix
approach beyond the two-parameter family to more general Fqm-linear combinations of
q-polynomials, where the structure matrices Γij are no longer circulant and closed-form
discriminants may not exist. A second direction is to determine, for prescribed hull
dimension h, whether the Frobenius family contains members that are simultaneously
MRD in the rank metric; the interplay between the rank-distance bound and the hull
constraint is not yet understood. Finally, the quantum coding interpretation (Remark 6.16)
raises the question of whether the families studied here can be used to construct EA-
QECCs meeting a Gilbert–Varshamov-type bound with prescribed ebit count, extending
the classical result of Sendrier [17] to the entanglement-assisted setting.
